One of the keys is the optimal consistency of honey dough for each particular honey cake. Let me cover the crucial questions.

What determines the consistency of honey dough?
- the amount of flour in its composition — the less flour you use, the more liquid and / or sticky the dough will be

- What are the types of honey dough consistencies?
- 1. Stiff
- 2. Soft
- 3. Liquid

title: STIFF HONEY DOUGH:
text:
▪obtained by adding a moderate amount of flour
▪should be slightly sticky when mixed
▪ready to work with (!!!) only after sitting for 15–20 minutes at room temperature — the fats contained in butter stabilize and the dough becomes non-sticky
▪rolled out with a rolling pin
▪easy, almost effortless to roll out

title: SOFT HONEY DOUGH:
text:
▪used for cake layers with a reduced flour content
▪turns out very sticky when mixed
▪ready to work with after 4–12 hours in the fridge (depending on the recipe) — during this time the fats become solid and stabilize completely –> the dough becomes non-sticky
▪easy to roll out with a rolling pin

title: LIQUID HONEY DOUGH (BATTER):
text:
▪contains the least amount of flour
▪ready to work with immediately after mixing
▪cannot be rolled out — for this batter you’ll need an offset spatula — evenly spread the batter over the parchment paper, giving it the desired shape

- What does the consistency of honey dough affect?
- the texture of finished cake layers

▪ crispy and crumbly cake layers are obtained from stiff dough
▪ soft dough ensures tender, soft and slightly airy cake layers
▪ honey batter helps to get elastic and at the same time very pliable cake layers

title: TEMPERATURE FOR ADDING BUTTER TO CARAMEL
text:
#marusya_theory_tips

Creamy caramel — a well-known to all confectioners and, seemingly, an easy-to-prepare French dessert, consisting of only 4 ingredients, in fact, is full of many secrets.

title: WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW ABOUT MOUSSES
text:
part 1

#marusya_about_mousse

Guys, today I’m presenting to you a new series of posts. Let's learn the science of making mousses from A to Z so you can feel confident when making them.

Let's start, as always, with the basics. What is a mousse?

Mousse (from French 'mousse' – “foam”) is a dish or a filling for cakes and other desserts with the consistency of an airy, light foam, composed of:

1. flavoring component (base)
2. whipped component (aerator)
3. thickener

Now let's take a closer look at each component.

- MOUSSE BASE is the main flavoring component which can be:

- custard
- ganache
- fruit puree
- creamy caramel
- nut or flower paste
- yogurt or fermented baked milk (ryazhenka)
- coffee/tea/alcohol

There are mousses with a “pure” base, i.e. only one ingredient is used, for example, caramel. But in my opinion, the most interesting are mousses with complex bases – you can combine coffee with fruit puree, caramel with nut paste or even crème anglaise with alcohol!

The mousse base takes up ~35-55% of the total mass, depending on the thickness of the base and the desired consistency of the finished mousse.

- WHIPPED COMPONENT OR AERATOR is responsible for airiness and lightness of the mousse. These aerators can be:

- whipping cream
- meringue
- pâte à bombe

- Pâte à bombe – a cream made of whipped egg yolks and boiled sugar syrup.

Before being added to the mousse, any of these ingredients is whipped to incorporate air bubbles, which helps to make the product airy and fluffy.

Meringue-based mousses

- most often, the Italian meringue is used, as it’s the most stable of all types of meringue
- contain the greatest number of air bubbles, and therefore are the most unstable, soft and delicate
- have the shortest shelf life
- keep maximum taste of the flavoring base
part 2

#marusya_about_mousse

Thanks to a large number of pluses under yesterday's post, I decided to immediately write a continuation – it's always nice to see mutual interest

Cream-based mousses

- make the taste of the mousse base less prominent, unlike meringue-based mousses
- more stable and thicker than those made with meringue
- use cold 30–33% cream
- whip it into soft peaks at medium speed – fast whipping leads to a less stable foam
- stick to the whipping temperature – 0–5 °C – if the temperature is at least 3–4 °C higher, the cream will whip much worse or may even curdle
- it’s important not to over-whip the cream, otherwise it’ll be difficult to combine it with the base, and the texture of the mousse won’t be perfect
- the temperature of the base to which we add the whipped cream shouldn’t exceed 35 °C, otherwise the mousse will turn out to be too liquid

It’s not common to use pure pâte à bombe to make mousses – most often it’s combined with cream or meringue.

In general, in one mousse you can use:

▪whipped cream and meringue
▪meringue and pâte à bombe
▪whipped cream and pâte à bombe
▪whipped cream, meringue and pâte à bombe

The whipped component can take up around 35–60% of the total mass of the mousse, depending on the thickness of the base, the type of aeration and the desired consistency of the finished mousse.

- THICKENER: traditionally, mousses are made with gelatin. However, some of the recipes call for agar-agar or cocoa butter, or gelatin + cocoa butter. The more gelatin you add, the thicker the mousse will be, and vice versa.

Gelatin can take up 0.5–2% of the total mass of the mousse:

▪ if the mousse contains alcohol, tart fruits or lots of air (meringue-based mousses), the percentage of gelatin will be around 2%
▪ mousses made from milk or white couvertures (chocolate with a high content of cocoa butter), contain around 0.5% gelatin
▪if it’s a chocolate-based mousse which contains enough cocoa butter (couverture/dark/bitter chocolate), you can skip adding the gelatin

title: PISTACHIO PASTE: 2 TIPS YOU DIDN'T KNOW ABOUT
text:
Pistachio paste has been added to all the desserts you see in the carousel, whether it be crémeux, cream for coating, cream cheese layer or frosting used between layers.

For me, it was extremely important to get a beautiful pistachio color and, at the same time, a pronounced yet natural pistachio taste.

What is more, the addition of delipaste balances out the slight bitterness of natural pistachio paste, and you get a pleasant taste reminiscent of pistachio ice cream.

- delipaste is a concentrated flavoring paste that gives a pronounced taste, aroma and color of a certain product to a dessert.

title: HOW TO TEMPER EGGS AND WHY YOU NEED TO
text:
part 1

#marusya_theory_tips

Every year I become more convinced that eggs are one of the most interesting products in the confectionery world!

This post is about egg tempering. I'll tell you how to temper the eggs and, more importantly, why we need to.

I think you immediately started to wonder:

- Tempering eggs? How come? It's all about chocolate!
- In fact, in the confectionery world, the word "tempering" has 2 meanings:

- 1st — it’s the process of heating and cooling chocolate to certain temperatures in order to obtain stable cocoa butter crystals responsible for giving the chocolate a glossy look and a nice crunch;

- 2d — it’s the process of slowly heating the eggs.

Scientifically, this method can be described as follows:

TEMPERING EGGS means slowly combining beaten cold or room-temperature eggs with a hot liquid without scrambling or curdling the eggs in the process.

title: HOW TO TEMPER EGGS (IN BRIEF)
text:
1. Slowly stream the hot/boiling liquid into the cold/room-temperature eggs while whisking.
2. Pour the warm eggs back into the saucepan.
part 2

#marusya_theory_tips

In a previous post, we discussed with you what tempering eggs is. So where does this process take place?

In fact, it’s quite simple and, most likely, you have already tempered eggs without knowing it. We temper eggs when we prepare the base for custards, pudding, ice cream, flan, crème brûlée, etc.

In the preparation of any custard, for example, there’s a step of trickling hot milk or cream into the egg mixture — when gradually adding a hot liquid to the eggs, we thereby temper them.

title: WHY WE NEED TO TEMPER EGGS
text:
Tempering eggs prevents the proteins from coagulating. Eggs are very sensitive to temperature. If you combine the eggs with hot liquid in one go, they will curdle. Therefore, when tempering, 2 rules must be observed:

- add the hot liquid gradually, in a thin stream
- constantly stir the mixture with a whisk

Lastly, let’s analyze one more interesting nuance.

title: HOW MUCH HOT LIQUID SHOULD BE ADDED TO EGGS
text:
Tempering is a means of getting something (eggs) from point A to point B (from cold to hot) slowly and steadily. And is a technique, not a scientific formula, which is why there’s no definitive answer for this question.

But there is no need to add all the hot liquid to the eggs — you should add just enough liquid to make the eggs hot (not warm, but hot!). You can then safely pour the tempered eggs into the saucepan with the remaining hot liquid. Just do not forget to stir with a whisk until the mixture becomes homogeneous.

title: HYDROCOLLOIDS IN CONFECTIONERY ART
text:
part 1

#marusya_hydrocolloids

The other day, while searching for useful information about the functions of sugar in shortcrust pastry, I came across an interesting block "Modern techniques in confectionery art", devoted to hydrocolloids.

Let's figure out what they are.

Basically, hydrocolloids are a heterogeneous group of long chain polymers (polysaccharides and proteins) characterized by their property of forming viscous dispersions and/or gels when dispersed in water.

It may sound confusing, but most of them are familiar to you. In simple terms, hydrocolloids are stabilizers and thickeners, derived from animal and plant sources.

Hydrocolloids of animal origin include the well-known gelatin. But I suggest having a closer look at hydrocolloids of vegetable origin.

Hydrocolloids derived from plant sources include:
- agar-agar
- pectin
- carrageenans
- gellan gum
- metilgel/methylcellulose
- sodium alginate
- tapioca maltodextrin
- xanthan gum
- guar gum

I think most of you only know the agar-agar and pectin from this list.

Pastry enthusiasts obsessed with confectionery could have seen the rest on the labels of bright, colorful and alluring SOSA bottles.

Or on white, plain and strict but no less attractive large containers with a red lid from LOUIS FRANCOIS, arranged in beautiful rows in the DGF boutique.

Those who are not into the confectionery business and are not familiar with the brands mentioned above, may remember some of the stabilizers and thickeners from the compositions of dairy and meat products.

So why, where and how are hydrocolloids used in modern confectionery production?

First of all, they are used as thickeners, of course, — to obtain gels, jellies, sauces, jams and other stable fillings. This is well known to everyone. But few people know that with the help of vegetable hydrocolloids, you can make ...

Can you guess the answer? Type it in the comments section.

part 2

#marusya_hydrocolloids

Judging by the answers in the comments section under the previous part of this post, you don’t know much about the application of hydrocolloids in modern cuisine. Let's try to change this.

So, here is a list of the most interesting and unusual, in my opinion, applications of plant-derived hydrocolloids:

- crispy dry foams made from milk and juices

In the meantime, let's get acquainted with the most mysterious representative of hydrocolloids of vegetable origin.

title: Carrageenan
text:
- extracted from some red seaweeds
- thermally reversible
- dissolves in cold water when mixed with sugar
- melting point 80ºC
- setting point 70ºC
- catalyst – calcium / potassium (usually in dairy products)

Functions:
- turns sauces into gels (rigid or elastic, tough or tender)

- increases the viscosity of liquids – is used, for example, in soy milk to give it a milk-like texture (without carrageenan it would have the consistency of water)

- suspends particles in liquid – is used, for example, in chocolate milk, so that solid cocoa particles do not settle at the bottom

- is used as a vegetable substitute for gelatin to stabilize mousses and frostings (mix the carrageenan powder with sugar and add to a cold liquid, then bring it to a boil, pour into molds and allow to stabilize)

title: EVERYTHING YOU NEED TO KNOW ABOUT GANASHES
text:
part 1

#marusya_about_ganache

I wanted to post a brief instruction on how to make chocolate ganache, but when I started writing, I realized that this topic requires more than one post. So welcome the new series of posts

Let's start, as always, with the basics.

- What is ganache?

Ganache is a mixture (emulsion) of chocolate (white, milk or dark) and liquid.

Ganache is made using a hot method — you heat the liquid and pour it over chocolate, after which you allow the ganache to cool.

What exactly is meant by liquid?

If on the Internet you come across an article that says that there are three types of ganache — made with heavy cream, butter and heavy cream with the addition of butter — you can immediately close the tab, since the author has only superficial knowledge about such an interesting product as ganache.

Firstly, the liquid in ganache can be represented by:

▪milk
▪heavy cream
▪fruit or berry juice
▪fruit or berry puree
▪and even crème anglaise or other custard

Secondly, in some cases, you can add to your ganache the following ingredients:

▪butter
▪sugar
▪all kinds of flavoring additives

Let’s continue.

Depending on the texture and purpose, the ganache can be thick or more runny:

▪ runny — is used for tarts and chocolates
▪ soft — can be used as an interlayer or filling for cakes, individual cakes or desserts
▪ thick — is used for bonbons and cake coating

The texture of the ganache can also be changed — it depends on the way you stir it — e.g, ganache can be whipped or made using the Chantilly cream method.

Ganache is a stable and balanced emulsion type chain in which fat molecules (in particular cocoa butter, milk fat, milk and/or heavy cream) are combined into a homogeneous substance together with water molecules thanks to emulsifiers present in chocolate (lecithin) and in heavy cream (proteins).

title: A CRASH COURSE IN CHOCOLATE
text:
part 1

Hello everyone! I have great news for you - today we are launching a series of articles about chocolate!

Even not being a chocolatier, almost every confectioner encounters chocolate when making cake decorating, ganaches, frostings, mousses, cremeux and other fillings. Therefore, acquaintance and building friendly relationships with a product such as chocolate will be relevant for many of you.

Let's start with the basics.

title: WHAT IS CHOCOLATE?
text: Chocolate is a confectionery product based on cocoa butter, which is a product of processing cocoa beans - the seeds of the chocolate tree, which are rich in theobromine and caffeine.

title: TYPES OF CHOCOLATE AND ITS COMPOSITION
text:
1. Black
2. Milk
3. White

The division is based on differences in composition, which determines the appearance of the product and its taste.

title: COMPOSITION OF BLACK CHOCOLATE
text:
- cocoa mass
- cocoa butter
- sugar

title: COMPOSITION OF MILK CHOCOLATE
text:
- cocoa mass
- cocoa butter
- sugar
- milk powder

title: COMPOSITION OF WHITE CHOCOLATE
text:
- cocoa butter
- sugar
- milk powder

*In fact, white chocolate isn’t really chocolate, as it doesn’t contain cocoa mass (cocoa beans). On this basis, the debate about whether to consider it real chocolate is still ongoing. I work with it all the time and refer it to chocolate, as due to the presence of cocoa butter in its composition, it has all the properties of chocolate.

title: WHAT ELSE CAN BE IN THE COMPOSITION OF CHOCOLATE:
text: In order for all the components to combine into a smooth emulsion, a small percentage of an emulsifier, such as soy lecithin, is often added to chocolate.

title: WHAT YOU SHOULD NOT HAVE IN CHOCOLATE:
text:
Good chocolate should be free of vegetable oils, vanillin and any other by-products.

And now the SECRET INFORMATION which is in open access

- The percentage indicated on the chocolate packaging (70%, 54.5%, 33%) is the percentage of cocoa mass.

title: BUT
text:
- The percentage indicated on the WHITE chocolate packaging is the percentage of cocoa butter content.
part 2

Let's continue delving into the world of chocolate. In the previous post you’ve asked about the brands that I use, so I’ll tell you what I usually work with.

The main rule when choosing chocolate is to give preference to PROFESSIONAL CHOCOLATE to get a stable result. You can easily buy it at any confectionery store.

If any of you still think that professional chocolate is a hard-to-find and expensive product, I have good news for you. Currently, the professional chocolate market is represented by a huge number of brands, among which everyone can find an attractive price option.

It can be:

- DGF (France)
- Natra Cacao (Spain)
- Cacao Barry (France)
- Lubeca (Germany)
- Callebaut (Belgium)

Many chefs prefer a French premium chocolate Valrhona, known for its line of chocolate with unique flavors. Desserts and even whole lines of desserts based on Valrhona chocolate are being developed, as they already contain certain flavors and don’t need to add anything extra - neither food dyes, nor puree, nor any other supplements. Of course, it optimizes many processes.

Since the fact that not everyone has the opportunity to use such expensive chocolate, I prefer DGF or Callebaut chocolate. Though I also enjoy working with brands such as IRCA and Lubeca.

I'll tell you more about Callebaut.

It is Belgian chocolate with a well-adjusted balanced flavor and texture made exclusively using natural ingredients. It is pleasant and easy to work with it, due to its high quality, as well as the convenient form of callets (drops), which is universal for almost any confectionery purpose.

- The line of «Finest Belgian Chocolate» is fully handmade, from cacao beans roasting to chocolate
part 3

In the previous posts — #marusya_about_chocolate — we have covered the basics: definition of chocolate, its types, composition and brands.

With this knowledge, we can proceed to the next step — tempering.

title: WHAT IS TEMPERING?
text:
Tempering, or crystallization, is the process of heating and cooling chocolate to certain temperatures in order to obtain stable cocoa butter crystals, which gives the chocolate a number of important properties:

- gives chocolate a glossy finish and make it snap cleanly
- allows you to avoid undesirable imperfections on the surface of chocolate:
▪ sugar bloom — a whitish film what affects the tasting
▪ fat bloom — greyish or whitish streaks or spots of cocoa butter
- chocolate hardens much faster
- stays solid in warmer temperatures, as it has a higher melting point.

title: METHODS FOR TEMPERING CHOCOLATE:
text:
- classic (tabling)
- seeding (callets)
- Mycryo — powdered cocoa butter

title: CLASSIC TEMPERING METHOD
text:
The method requires you to use a marble or granite slab/countertop. Since not everyone has an access to it, I won’t dwell on it in detail. But the technique itself is important for understanding the processes:

Destroy the solid form of chocolate by bringing it to the melting point:
▪dark — 50-55°C
▪milk — 45-50°C
▪white — 40-45°C

- Bring it down to the crystallization temperature of cocoa butter — 27°C

- Bring the chocolate to its working temperature:
▪dark — 31-32°C
▪milk — 30-31°C
▪white — 29-30°C

- Give liquid chocolate the desired shape.

- Let the chocolate stabilize and become solid again.

title: SEEDING METHOD OR CALLET TEMPERING
text:
The trick is that the callets themselves are already tempered. Cocoa butter crystals are already crystallized, that is, step 2 from the classic method is omitted. All you need to do is melt the chocolate and bring it to working temperature.
part 4

We continue a detailed analysis of the methods for tempering chocolate.

As you remember from the previous post — #marusya_about_chocolate — the classic method is not the easiest one, since it requires lots of effort as well as marble or granite slab/countertop. But at the same time, this is the only way to temper chocolate in large quantities (over 1 kg).

In large scale production where it’s often necessary to temper 1-2 kg of chocolate or even more, they use special tempering machines that maintain the required temperature of chocolate.

For home bakers, one of the best methods is the seeding method or callet tempering. Let’s learn how it works.

Destroy the solid form of chocolate by bringing it to the melting point:
▪dark — 50–55 °C
▪milk — 45–50 °C
▪white — 40–45 °C

- Add chocolate callets and stir to bring the chocolate to its working temperature:
▪dark — 31–32 °C
▪milk — 30–31 °C
▪white — 29–30 °C

And voilà — you can give liquid chocolate the desired shape

With this method there is no need to first bring chocolate down to the crystallization temperature of cocoa butter (27 °C), and then bring it up to the working temperature, as with the classic method, since the callets themselves are already tempered and have a stable crystalline structure.

- If I use chocolate callets only, then I just melt them and that's it?

Even if you use only chocolate in callets, bringing it to working temperature is not enough — heat treatment destroys the bonds between cocoa butter molecules, the crystalline structure breaks up and collapses.

That’s why it is necessary to add cold callets with a stable crystalline structure to melted chocolate, as they prompt the chain reaction resulting in properly crystallized chocolate.
part 5

Secrets of tempering chocolate using seeding method (callets)

1. It is best to melt chocolate in the microwave. Chocolate is very hygroscopic, meaning it absorbs moisture from the air. Therefore, a water bath will not be the best option for melting chocolate.

2. To avoid overheating, melt the chocolate in the microwave in 20 to 30 second intervals, thoroughly stirring it with a spatula between each interval.

- melt the white chocolate on the lowest power level and in very short, 10-20 second intervals as it can be easily overheated

3. I do not recommend melting chocolate in glassware — glass retains temperature for a long time and gives it to chocolate even after we’ve already brought it to 50-55 °C (45-50 °C milk and 40-45 °C white chocolate). Opt for plastic vessels instead.

4. Chocolate must be constantly stirred! This is necessary in order to ensure the same temperature of chocolate at the bottom, sides and in the middle of the bowl, as well as to correctly measure the temperature. It is most convenient to measure the temperature of chocolate with a pyrometer.

5. In order to bring the chocolate to its working temperature (dark — 31-32 °C, milk — 30-31 °C, white — 29-30 °C), add callets to the melted chocolate (20-25% of the total volume). With this amount, stable crystals will prompt the chain reaction resulting in properly crystallized chocolate.

This ratio is considered optimal, but since there are many variables in this equation, I would call it only approximate. You can be guided by it, but make sure to always keep an eye on the temperature of the chocolate.

6. When you get down to work, please remember that:

- You need to work with chocolate quickly — if the chocolate is properly tempered, it will set in 3 minutes at a temperature of about 20 °C
- white chocolate is much thicker than dark or milk chocolate — to make it easier to work with, add a little cocoa butter along with the callets to it
part 6

#marusya_about_chocolate

Today I suggest talking about a very interesting product, which has no analogues on the market at the moment — Mycryo.

title: WHAT IS MYCRYO?
text:
Mycryo® is the brand name of the Barry Callebaut group of companies, which specializes in the production of a unique product — pure cocoa butter in powder form.

This 100% vegetable fat is an absolutely healthy product, mostly thanks to cocoa beans: it contains no cholesterol, has low calorie content, and you need less fat for frying.

If you look at the original packaging of Mycryo, you will see a photo of a delicious steak. And there’s a reason for that. Mycryo has a number of unique properties that make the range of its application very diverse:

- it resists frying temperatures better than butter or oils, and doesn't burn
- brings out the natural flavors of even the most delicate ingredients, and unlike other fats, it does not dominate over them
- and, of course, facilitates the process of chocolate tempering

title: HOW IS MYCRYO OBTAINED?
text:
Cocoa butter, obtained through roasting and grinding cocoa beans, is then frozen at very low temperatures to produce a dry powder. In other words, atomization occurs — dry powder is cooled to approximately -250 °C.

As a result, cocoa butter takes the form of granules, which are pure beta crystals, which are essential for proper chocolate tempering.

Let’s try to figure it out.

title: TYPES OF COCOA BUTTER CRYSTALS
text:
So, there are six types of cocoa butter crystals, each with a name: γ‎ (gamma), α (alpha), β'' (beta 2), β' (beta prime), β (beta) and super-β (super-beta).

They differ from each other by the strength of the bonds between the molecules. The stronger the bonds are, the more energy (higher temperature) is needed to break these bonds.

Of all six crystals, only one fits for tempering — beta (β) — they are the most stable and form the correct crystal lattice.
part 7

#marusya_about_chocolate

Chocolate tempering with Mycryo — the conventional technique VS method I use.

You asked me for the details, so there you are.

title: CONVENTIONAL TECHNIQUE FOR CHOCOLATE TEMPERING WITH MYCRYO
text:
1. Melt the chocolate to 40-45 °C in a microwave oven or over a water bath.
2. Leave the chocolate to cool (to 34-35 °C for dark chocolate or 33-34 °C for milk, white or colored chocolate) at room temperature.
3. Add Mycryo (1% of the chocolate mass), mix thoroughly.
4. Once the chocolate has reached an ideal temperature (31-32 °C for dark chocolate or 29-30 °C for milk, white or colored chocolate), use the product.
5. To use the chocolate for a longer time, keep it at 31-32 °C in the case of dark chocolate or 29-30 °C in the case of milk, white or colored chocolate.

title: MY CHOCOLATE TEMPERING METHOD USING MYCRYO
text:
1. Melt the chocolate to 40-45 °C in the microwave
- It is better not to use a water bath — chocolate is very hygroscopic

2. Add ~15-20% callets of the total chocolate mass and mix thoroughly until they have completely dissolved, lowering the temperature to 35 °C.
- Cooling chocolate at room temperature takes a long time and it must be constantly stirred, otherwise the crystallization will be uneven — chocolate cools much faster on the walls of the bowl.

- 3. Sift Mycryo through a fine sieve to get rid of large pieces — when adding Mycryo, the temperature of the chocolate drops rapidly, so you need to combine the chocolate with cocoa butter into a homogeneous mass very quickly, which makes it difficult for large pieces of Mycryo to get in.

4. Add Mycryo (2% of the chocolate mass), stir thoroughly.
- Earlier on the official website it was indicated that 1% Mycryo is enough, but recently the manufacturer has changed the proportion to 2% — that is, 2 g of Mycryo per 100 g of chocolate.

- 5. see step 4 of the conventional technique
- 6. see step 5 of the conventional technique

title: ALL YOU NEED TO KNOW ABOUT STARCH
text:
#marusya_about _starch

We’ve already talked about pectin, agar-agar and gelatin. So today I suggest talking about the most popular thickening agent — starch.

In fact, there are lots of types of starch: potato, rice, wheat, corn, tapioca, sorghum, etc. However, the most common types are potato and cornstarch.

It is preferable to use cornstarch for making desserts, and it’s not recommended to replace it with potato starch. Cornstarch ensures a more delicate texture, while adding potato starch results in a much thicker texture.

Potato starch
- ensures a more fluid texture
- has a characteristic flavor
- the starch mixture is transparent
- may impart a bluish color to some dishes

Cornstarch
- ensures a more viscous texture
- has no aftertaste
- the starch mixture is turbid
- does not change the color of the dish

Types of cornstarch
- regular cornstarch — does not contain impurities and has a white color
- modified starch — a safe product, additionally processed for better absorption

Take into account thatstarch as a thickener activates properly only after bringing the mixture to a boil

The boiling point of mixtures with starch added is 82 °C.

Bring the filling or custard with cornstarch to a boil, then, stirring vigorously with a spatula, allow it to cook over low heat for several minutes so that the starch has completely denatured — subjected to a heat treatment, the starch granules should swell and change their structure.

If the starch has not completely swollen, after cooling, the filling won’t be stable and may leak water, acquiring a liquid, runny structure.

The dosage of starch may be different depending on:

- density of the product to be thickened: liquid with a high percentage of water or a thicker puree with a high content of natural pectin
- consistency of the filling you want to get

title: HOW TO CORRECTLY MAKE AND SERVE A CAKE WITH BUTTERCREAM
text:
#marusya_theory_tips

It hasn’t been long since a new Napoleon cake recipe set was released, and I’ve already received lots of similar feedback: “The cake is delicious, but I didn’t like the buttercream — it’s heavy and too greasy.”

- Can Napoleons and other cakes with buttercream taste like this?

- No, there isn’t

There are 2 reasons why your buttercream can turn out to be heavy and greasy:

1. You didn’t follow the buttercream preparation instructions properly
2. You served the cake with buttercream inappropriately

So, let's learn how to get the best results.

title: HOW TO MAKE THE PERFECT BUTTERCREAM:
text:
- make sure your butter is soft
- whip the butter on maximum speed of your mixer
- the whipping time should be from 3–5 to 10–15 minutes, depending on the power of your mixer and the amount of butter (it’s impossible to over whip the buttercream)
- if you’re making a cake for yourself, I advise you to try using 72% butter instead of 82% — this way you will get a lighter version of the buttercream

- At a result, properly whipped butter should increase in volume by 2 times and become lighter. Well whipped butter will allow you to get a light, airy and not greasy buttercream.

title: HOW SHOULD THE CAKE WITH BUTTERCREAM BE SERVED:
text:
- in no case do we serve the cake immediately from the fridge, as the fat molecules harden at this temperature
- you should take a well stabilized cake out of the fridge and slice it into portions
- keep the slices at room temperature for 10 to 30 minutes, depending on the temperature in the room, so that the buttercream softens
- and only then serve the cake to the client, guest or enjoy the cake yourself

- A properly served cake keeps its shape well, and has a light, airy buttercream

title: HONEY. MYTHS VS REALITY
text:
part 1

Since without honey a honey cake is no longer a honey cake, I’ve been working with this product a lot for at least several years.

Therefore, I’ve faced a wide range of questions regarding this ingredient. The most popular of them are the following:

- Can honey be heated? Doesn’t it become toxic after this?

- What are the substitutes for honey in recipes and how to use them correctly?

Honey is a healthy and natural product. It contains glucose, fructose, a small amount of sucrose, flavonoids, microelements and enzymes. It has bactericidal and medicinal properties.

- So, the first question and the most common myth at the same time.

- When heated, honey becomes toxic.

Honey won’t become toxic, no matter how long you heat it: it does not initially contain any toxic components that are dangerous to humans.

In fact, an organic compound known as 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) is formed when honey is heated. There is an opinion that this compound is highly toxic, that's why it’s dangerous to heat honey.

Let's see how toxic this compound is, and whether we risk to get food poisoning from eating a piece of honey cake or adding honey to hot tea.

HMF is an intermediate product of the breakdown of sugars in an acidic medium, which increases with heating, that is, HMF appears in absolutely all products where sugars have undergone heat treatment in the presence of acid.

Therefore, HMF is found in any baked goods, jams, roasted apples and beets, roasted coffee, soda, and often in quantities ten times greater than in honey.

Why, then, is there GOST (State Standard) that regulates the norm of HMF in honey? - let’s figure it out in the continuation of the article

P.S. The photos show a honey cheesecake "Baklava". And yes, there is a lot of honey in it and it was baked at 170-180 °С / 338-356 °F
part 2

So, we already know that an organic compound 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) is formed when honey is heated and it’s neither toxic, nor carcinogenic.

So why are there GOST (State Standard) recommendations according to which the HMF concentration in honey should not exceed 25 mg/kg ?!

The limit for oxy methyl furfural in honey was set not to protect people from a "toxic" product, but to ensure that the product has not undergone overheating during processing.

This indicator is mainly used by honey processors when purchasing lots of honey and helps to determine its age, as well as whether this honey has been overheated during presale processing.

Deviation from the norm characterizes not the danger of heated honey, but rather its uselessness, since enzymes and proteins denaturation takes place much earlier than HMF appears. In this sense, those who like to put honey into hot tea have nothing to worry about, except that honey will lose its medicinal properties.

In any case, after putting a teaspoon of honey into your hot drink, all antioxidants won’t disappear at once - they simply won’t have time to do it, because your mug is not an autoclave.

Perhaps no one has studied the effect of HMF on human health and its long-term consequences. But taking into account our daily use of a wide variety of products with HMF throughout our lives, this organic compound should not cause serious concerns.

When heated, other organic compounds can form in honey that are harmful to the body (or affect it ambiguously), however, they do not make heated honey noticeably more toxic than almost any other food that you fry or bake.

Moreover, due to the acidic environment (pH 3.5), HMF also appears in raw honey.

In the continuation of the article, we"ll analyze why citric acid is sometimes added to the dough for a honey cake and what can be used instead of honey.

part 3

While I was reparing materials for the articles on my site, I found out that one very interesting topic was not fully disclosed.

Almost a year and a half ago I started writing an article about honey, and in the first two parts I gave a detailed answer to such a tricky question as to whether it's possible to heat honey and whether it becomes harmful after that.

If you are not familiar with this information or want to refresh it in your memory, follow the hashtag #marusya_about_honey.

Today I'd like to analyze another important question:

- What are honey substitutes and how to use them in the recipe?

Allergy prevents some people from consuming this product, that's why we need to find a suitable replacement.

title: ATTENTION
text:
The allergens present in honey are subjected to heat treatment during baking, after which most of them break down, and in most cases, cease to cause an allergic reaction!

However, if you want to be 100% sure or cook to order for an allergic client, there are 3 main replacement options:
- glucose-fructose or glucose syrup
- trimoline
- artificial honey

You can read more about these ingredients here #marusya_about_sugar .

- Approximate ratios of replacing honey with glucose / glucose-fructose syrup / artificial honey — 1:1; trimoline — 1:0.75

Also, sometimes honey is replaced with maple or rice syrup, molasses, agave nectar. As you can see, there are lots of options.

Many people often ask another question:

- Can I replace sugar with honey?

When replacing sugar with honey, remember that it's sweeter than sugar. In addition, sugar and honey have different densities, so a 1:1 substitution will make your baked goods not only very sweet, but also sticky, heavy, and overly moist.

- Ratios of replacing sugar with honey

For every 100 g sugar indicated in the recipe, use 75 g honey.
part 4

#marusya_about_honey

Guys, thank you for being so active under the previous post — I see that the topic of honey is really interesting for you, and therefore I decided not to put off writing the continuation.

- Things to remember when replacing sugar with honey:

- increase baking time as the dough becomes more “heavy” and needs to be baked longer
- lower the temperature by 15 °C, as honey gives the dough a darker color
- reduce the amount of liquid in the recipe; reduce or increase the amount of flour

Summing up, it’s definitely possible to replace sugar with honey. However, be sure to stick to the right ratio and, if necessary, make adjustments based on the thickness, consistency and sweetness of the honey used.

- Why add citric acid or lemon juice to honey dough?

Adding citric acid is an optional step in the preparation of honey dough and it's just to be on the safe side in case baking soda fails to react properly. If it hasn't activated, you may face several issues:

- smell of baking soda during baking
- bitter aftertaste in cakes
- cake with frosting / berry or fruit filling can be streaked blue — frosting or filling contains acid that reacts with not activated baking soda in the cake layers
- flat, thin crepe-like cake layers

I advise you not to neglect this step, since there is always a possibility that the soda won’t react properly for the following reasons:

- different composition of natural honey (more/less acidic, more or less acid in the composition of different types of honey)
- different composition of alkalized cocoa (more/less acidic, more or less acid in the composition of cocoa with varying degrees of alkalization)
- wrong temperature that doesn’t ensure a proper reaction between baking soda and acid

- Ratio of adding lemon juice to honey dough

1-1.5 g per every 100 g of dough

Part 2

#marusya_about_ganache

One of the last posts of 2022 was the dedicated to ganache theory. I am very pleased that you liked that post, so here’s the continuation

As we have already discussed, ganache is a mixture of chocolate and liquid. Now let's talk in detail about the chocolate used to make ganaches.

The following types of chocolate can be used for making ganaches:
▪white
▪milk
▪dark
▪bitter

Chocolate can be used in any form:
▪chocolate bars (tablets)
▪chocolate blocks (chunks)
▪chocolate callets (chips)
▪chocolate drops

I usually work with callets, as they help to speed up the melting of chocolate when in contact with hot liquid.

- the main requirement is that callets should be stored in sealed packaging, protected from moisture — if water gets into chocolate, its shelf life decreases and the quality of the product deteriorates

Impact factors

title: Ganache Components: Liquid, Butter, Sugar, and Additives
text:
TEXTURE
▪ thanks to the cocoa butter, ganache becomes fluid when heated and sets when cooled (due to the crystallization of cocoa butter molecules)
▪the lower the cocoa butter content and the higher the sugar content are, the softer the consistency of the ganache is

- for making ganache the chocolate should contain at least 18% cocoa butter and 40-70% cocoa products (these figures are usually indicated by manufacturers on the packaging)

- By cocoa products I mean the content of cocoa butter and cocoa mass (cocoa powder).

TASTE
▪ characteristic flavor of chocolate:

- white – sweet milky
- milk – vanilla-caramel
- dark – rich chocolate

▪ characteristic chocolate bitterness: it reinforces in ganache due to the increased content of cocoa products (70% or more) and is leveled when the content of cocoa products is around 50% (medium).
part 3

#marusya_about_ganache

Apart from chocolate, ganache must contain liquid. But here is where it gets fun: you can use different liquids, e.g:

- Fresh or pasteurized cream

The fat content of cream should be 35-40%. Thanks to minimal heat treatment, the finished ganache will have a rich creamy taste, but at the same time ‒ a reduced shelf life.

- Sterilized or UHT cream

The fat content is 35-37%. These types of cream are exposed to high temperatures for a short period of time. This process extends the product's shelf life making these creams chefs’ favorites when working with ganaches.

Milk
Is used to replace some or all of the cream in ganache. Unsweetened condensed milk (also called evaporated or concentrated milk) is often used to reduce the amount of water added, which negatively affects the shelf life of the ganache.

- Fruit or berry puree

Part of the cream can be replaced with puree. Most often, the ratio of puree and cream is 1:1. It is added to give ganache a fruity flavor and aroma, as well as interesting vivid colors.

DOSAGE
▫milk: maximum 40%
▫cream: 20-50%
▫puree: maximum 50%

How the liquid added affects the ganache?

TEXTURE
◽ gives the ganache a silky, melting texture during tasting (provided the fat content is at least 35%)
◽ in some cases, e.g. when preparing whipped ganache, cream is a necessary element for increasing the volume, as well as trapping and stabilizing air bubbles in the finished ganache

MOISTURE CONTENT
◽ liquid with a water content of about 60% dissolves sugar and makes the chocolate less dense

TASTE
▫ due to the fat molecules present in the composition, it has aroma-retaining properties and is a carrier of taste to our receptors
Part 4

So, did you miss this series of posts?

Today we continue talking about ganaches and as usual, I’m ready to share with you a concentrate of the best information from top pastry chefs and chocolatiers, seen through the prism of my experience and critical thinking.

Check out the beginning here #marusya_about_ganache

We’ve already analyzed the chocolate and liquid in the composition of ganache in detail, now let's move on to possible additives.

Butter
- fat content — 82% and more — the more fat contained in butter, the longer the shelf life of the finished ganache will be
- the butter is added when the ganache is at 32–34ºС

- dose — 5–15%

- recommended dose of fats (butter + cocoa butter) — 25–40% — too much fats will destabilize the ganache (the emulsion will break), while insufficient amount of fats will result in a ganache that’s too thick

When added to a ganache, the butter influences its:

TEXTURE
▪when the butter is heated, the consistency of the ganache becomes runnier, and when it cools, the ganache becomes thicker
▪makes the ganache smooth and creamy, adds it a glossy shine, as well as a delicate, melt-in-the mouth texture (provided the butter is added at the end of cooking, at 30-35ºС, without prior melting).

TASTE
▪ has aroma-retaining properties and is a carrier of taste to our receptors due to fat molecules in the composition
▪ reduces the bitterness of chocolate with a high content of cocoa products, e.g., >70%.

SHELF LIFE
▪ adding butter to cream before boiling it prolongs the shelf life of the ganache, and also contributes to the even distribution of fat molecules in the mixture.
Part 5

#marusya_about_ganache

In the previous part we discussed all the nuances of adding butter to a ganache. But apart from it, the following ingredients can be added to the ganache, namely:

Sugar
- sugar in ganaches can be represented by: sucrose (=sugar), invert sugar or glucose syrup (high in dextrose)
- dose — at least 25% of the total weight

When added to a ganache, sugar influences its:

TASTE
▪makes the ganache sweeter

TEXTURE
▪makes it softer and more elastic
▪increases the viscosity of the ganache, making it more stable due to its hygroscopic properties

SHELF LIFE
▪ prolongs shelf life — sugar helps to “bind” water present in cream, making it unavailable for the microorganisms (molds) to multiply.

- Sorbitol or food supplement E420
It is an odorless white crystalline powder with a pleasant taste. It is two times less sweet than regular sugar and is very hygroscopic (absorbs and retains moisture).
- dose — 1.5–2.5% of the total weight

The way sorbitol affects the ganache is similar to sugar, however, E420 is used primarily as a stabilizer, and not as a sweetener.

Aromatic additives
- can be represented by various extracts, essential oils, alcohol, as well as flavored cream or milk
- all additives that are sensitive to microflora (cocoa powder, spices, etc.) should be boiled for several minutes along with the cream
Part 6 and last

Guys, have you missed us?

‘cause we missed you immensely!

Inspired after a short vacation, we are preparing new wow-materials for you!

Today I’d like to share with you the last piece of information about ganaches in order you could round up all the information you already learnt and arrange it into a coherent picture.

We have already discussed with you what ganache is, what it can consist of and what are the possible additives, and we also examined in detail each basic component separately: the recommended dosage of the ingredient and its influence on the texture, taste and shelf life of the ganache.

Check out the beginning here #marusya_about_ganache

Today I will share with you a couple more useful tips and tricks.

- Why has your ganache split?

1. It doesn't contain enough liquid
2. Poor dispersion of fats in water
3. Indoor temperature is too high

🆘 How to fix split ganache?

1. Add heavy cream/milk/puree
2. Process the mixture with a hand blender
3. Process the mixture with a hand blender and allow it to cool

And here comes another interesting nuance:

- Ganache should be processed with a hand blender while it is hot to avoid air bubbles getting into the mixture! This is due to the fact that:

- air is a favorable environment for microorganisms
- fats that are in contact with air eventually turn rancid

- How and how long can ganache be stored?

- Before storing and cooling the ganache, it should be covered with cling film that comes in contact with the surface of the ganache. This way, you will protect your ganache from air, microorganisms and evaporation of aromatic substances.

- Ganaches can be stored in the fridge at 4ºС for no more than 2 days. You can freeze them only in finished products.

title: WHY DO YOU NEED TO SIFT THE FLOUR?
text:
Almost every pastry recipe calls for sifted flour. Have you ever thought about why you should sift it?

Let's start with what we have actually moved away from for a long time, thanks to modern production technologies.

In the past, it was always necessary to sift the flour in order to:

▪ get rid of weevils and other bugs
- Nowadays contaminated foods should be disposed immediately.
▪ get rid of the smallest pieces of stone for grinding grain — quern. The saddle quern consisted of a flat stone bed and a rounded stone to be operated manually against it; later, millstones developed from those hand-operated querns
▪ get rid of debris — threads from packing bags, cereals from a neighboring box, pieces of paper or plastic bags, etc.

Nowadays, here are a few times you should sift your flour for baking:

▪ to eliminate and prevent lumps — when your flour has been sitting around for a while, seems to be tightly packed, or has been stored at high humidity, lumps form even in high-quality flour.
▪ to get a homogeneous, uniform base for the dough — sifted flour mixes better with other ingredients, and the dough behaves more predictably
▪ to get much lighter and airier flour — it’s especially important when baking sponges
▪ to guarantee you get the right amount when the recipe uses cups instead of grams as a unit of measure (American recipes) — sifted flour will have a larger volume than not sifted

title: Lifehack from Marusya
text: If the flour you are using is fairly fresh and does not contain any lumps, in most cases you can skip sifting, and make your flour airier simply by mixing it with a whisk.

title: Honey Cake Layers: Factors That Affect the Intensity of Honey Taste and Aroma
text:
HONEY CAKE LAYERS: FACTORS THAT AFFECT THE INTENSITY OF HONEY TASTE AND AROMA

Honey cake layers can have a different intensity of honey taste and aroma: from delicate, subtle honey notes to strong, pronounced ones. What does it depend on?

The very first and seemingly obvious answer that comes to mind is the amount of honey added. But in fact, this is far from the primary factor.

1. The intensity of the honey taste and aroma in the cake layers depends primarily on the heat treatment the batter undergoes before baking — the more you heat the honey mixture, the more pronounced taste will have the cake layers:

- subtle honey taste and aroma can be obtained by bringing the mixture for the honey dough to 60–70 °C over a water bath or in a saucepan
- moderately pronounced taste is obtained by bringing the honey or the honey mixture to a boil (100–116 °C)
- rich, pronounced honey taste and aroma of the cake layers is achieved by boiling the honey mixture or by using the dough made with burnt honey (> 116 °C)

2. Secondly, the intensity of the honey taste and aroma of the cake layers depends on the type of honey. If you want to get cakes with a light, delicate honey taste, opt for light types of honey, for example, acacia or linden. Buckwheat honey and other dark types should be preferred if you like cakes with a rich, pronounced honey taste.

3. The amount of honey added to the dough makes less difference to the intensity of honey taste and aroma of cake layers compared to the type of honey and its heat treatment. Therefore, do not be surprised that the amount of honey in honey recipes can vary from 60 to 450 g, depending on the recipe.

title: BROWN VS. WHITE EGGS — IS THERE A DIFFERENCE?
text:
#marusya_theory_tips

Guys, you probably noticed that in some countries in supermarkets the prices for brown and white eggs differ? Is there any reason for that? Or is it just a marketing ploy?

Let's figure it out. But first things first.

Is there really a difference between brown and white eggs?

- Yes — in color

Eggs come in many colors, depending on the breed of the hen. Chickens have different pigment genes that determine the color of the egg shell. Generally speaking, white shell eggs come from hens with white feathers and white earlobes, while brown shell eggs are produced by hens with brown feathers and red earlobes.
- some chickens have a unique pigment gene and lay multi-colored eggs — light blue, green and even pink

- No — in terms of nutritional value and taste

The color of the eggshell is not indicative of the best quality of the egg. In fact, there is no distinguishable difference between brown and white eggs when it comes to taste and nutritional value.
- The nutritional value and palatability of an egg depend solely on the diet and environment of the chicken. The food eaten by the hen can directly affect how an egg tastes, which means that pasture-raised hens usually lay eggs that have a richer taste and higher concentration of useful macro- and microelements

- Is the higher price for brown eggs a marketing ploy?

- No — hens with brown feathers tend to be larger than hens with white feathers, meaning they consume more feed. Therefore, brown eggs need to be sold at a higher price to make up for the extra costs

- Yes — if you have faced an unscrupulous dealer speculating on their more "natural" appearance

title: HOW TO RECALCULATE THE CHOCOLATE PERCENTAGE
text:
#marusya_about_chocolate

More than enough times, I've been faced with complaints about broken ganache and tearful pleas for help.

I will help.

In 99% of cases, beginners simply replace the amount of chocolate specified in the recipe with exactly the same amount of chocolate with a different percentage of cocoa products.

title: DON’T DO THIS
text:
Is it possible basically to replace one chocolate with another?

- Yes, if you correctly calculate the required amount of chocolate with a cocoa butter content that is different from that specifed in the recipe

Let's say the recipe says 400 g of dark chocolate 54% (chocolate A). You only have 64% chocolate (Chocolate B) available.

How to recalculate?

The 54% marking reflects the total content of cocoa products (cocoa butter and cocoa liquor). For instance, 100 g of 54% chocolate may contain 45 g of sugar (45%), 19 g of cocoa liquor (19%) and 36 g of cocoa butter (36%).
- see the cocoa butter content on the package or clarify with the manufacturer

Enter the factor value

factor = cocoa butter content/100

The recipe uses 400 g of 54% chocolate (which is 19% cocoa liquor and 36% cocoa butter), and you want to replace it with 64% chocolate, which contains 41% cocoa butter

factor A (chocolate 54%) = 36% (cocoa butter)/100 = 0.36
factor B (chocolate 64%) = 41% (cocoa butter)/100 = 0.41

We have calculated the factor value for both types of chocolate, now we need to calculate how much of the available chocolate 64% we will need, according to the formula:

x = (weight of chocolate A * factor A) / factor B

Substitute the values:

x = (400 g * 0.36) / 0.41 = 351 g

That is, you can replace 400 g of 54% chocolate with 351 g of 64% chocolate that you have available.

title: 8 TYPES OF BUTTER AND HOW TO USE THEM — 2

#marusya_about_butter

Any butter is made from cream. But depending on the origin of the cream, the composition of the butter and ways of preparation, there are several varieties that ensure different tastes of meals and serve for different purposes:

title: Sweet Cream Butter (Unsalted Butter)
text: It is the most popular variety due to its versatility: it can be used both for frying vegetables, meat, and for making desserts and pastries. It is made only from cream of animal origin.

title: Salted Butter
text: Unsalted butter is all cream, while the salted variety has some salt added. Salt acts as a preservative, so this variety of butter lasts longer than the unsalted one. Most often, it is used for spreading on bread, topping veggies and pasta.

title: Ghee butter
text: Gee is nothing more than the pure butterfat! It is cooked over low heat to remove the water molecules until the milk solids brown lightly, creating a slightly nutty, caramelized aroma. Ghee butter is shelf-stable and has a high smoke point. It is most commonly used for sautéing vegetables, meat, but it’s also used in baked goods thanks to its rich flavor.

title: Compound butter
text: This is a special variety of butter that has been softened to a pliable state, and then has herbs, spices, and/or sweeteners (fruit or berry purees) added to it. Usually chilled and then sliced, compound butter can add herby richness to a steak, enhance the flavor of a baked good, or add creaminess to a pasta sauce.

title: VARIETIES OF SALT
text:
There are 4 types of food salt:

▫table salt
▫rock salt
▫sea salt
▫lake salt

They differ from each other in the methods of harvesting, chemical composition — and, accordingly, taste, as well as varying degrees of salinity, depending on the content of sodium chloride in the composition.

title: ▪TABLE SALT
text:
The most commonly used variety of salt. Most table salt is mined, then put into water, purified of other trace minerals and re-dehydrated (evaporated). The content of NaCl is no less than 97% on a dry matter basis.

There are different grades of table salt:

- second
- first
- top
- "Extra"

The main feature of "Extra" grade is that it is fine-grained (almost like a powder) and often comes in "iodized" form which means it includes a small amount of potassium iodide or sodium iodide. The addition of iodine does not change the taste of the salt itself, but when heated above 100 °C, iodized salt decomposes and gives a dish a metallic aftertaste.

"Extra" grade salt has a distinctive taste. Such salt is convenient to use in food production: its high degree of salinity and low cost reduce the cost of purchasing and storing the product.

#marusya_about_salt

title: ▪ROCK SALT
text: It is considered natural: it is obtained by mining, then ground and it’s ready to be used. It has a less intense taste than that of table salt.

title: ▪SEA SALT
text:
A type of salt of natural (marine) origin, extracted from seawater through the use of a vacuum evaporation process after which it is sun and wind dried and then distilled into an edible, solid form. The purity of sea salt depends on the composition and purity of the sea water from which it is harvested.

Sea salt not only enhances the taste of foods, but can also add different flavors depending on the additives in its composition. It is much less salty than table or rock salt, so when cooking, you need much more of it to make the dish salty.

▫Fleur de Sel ("flower of salt" in French)
The most expensive among sea salts. It has an exceptional taste and is able to give dishes a special delicacy and sophistication. This salt has snowflake-like crystals which add a crunchy texture to dishes.

title: ▪LAKE SALT
text:
It is extracted from the bottom of salt lakes, where it settles naturally. Then it undergoes purification processes, after which the salt crystals are converted into food salt. Lake salt has a low sodium chloride content, so it is considered less salty.

Classification of salt on the basis of salinity levels from higher to lower:

1. Table salt "Extra" grade
2. Table salt of the first, second and top grades
3. Rock salt
4. Sea salt
5. Lake salt

In all my recipes I use rock salt. Therefore, if you use any other type of salt, make sure to reduce / increase its amount based on the degree of salinity.
part 3 and last

Today we will figure out how much salt should be added to desserts and pastries, and we will also talk about what kind of salt is used in confectionery.

How much salt to add? This usually depends on:

◾ variety of salt
We have already figured out that, first and foremost, the amount of salt added to dessert depends on the type of salt you use, since each of them has a different degree of salinity. You can read about it in detail by following the hashtag #marusya_about_salt

◾ goal you want to achieve
If you want just to enhance the taste of the dessert, then you will need less salt than to eliminate excessive sweetness, for example.

◾ your taste preferences
Depending on taste buds, a dessert with the same amount of salt will be moderately salty for some, and slightly over-salted for others.

- Basic ratios of salt to flour and sugar:
1/4 tsp. salt per cup (130 g) flour
1/4 tsp. salt per cup (180 g) sugar

If the dessert you are making contains both flour and sugar, then first use salt in ratio only to the ingredient that weighs more, check the result, and then add more salt if necessary.

- Which variety of salt to use in pastry?
When choosing the type of salt to add, think of the goal you want to achieve:

◾ if you need salt to decorate your dessert, then opt for Fleur de Sel — it has snowflake-like crystals and ennobles the dessert with its crispy texture. Other varieties of sea salt that have a crystalline structure are also suitable for decoration.

◾ to enhance the taste of the dessert, I advise you to use rock or sea salt. They dissolve well in the dough and don’t add bitterness, which is typical of iodized and table salt.

◾ if you use salt as a bitterness neutralizer, why add an extra bitter taste along with table salt?

title: WHY ADD SALT TO DESSERTS?
text:
part 1

When I began to study this question, it immediately became clear that for this topic I’ll need more than one post. You may wonder what salt has to do with dessert. Let’s have a look.

Firstly, in some cases it’s really impossible to make a dessert without salt. Secondly, without it, most of sweet pastries become insipid.

Let's figure it out.

title: FUNCTIONS OF SALT IN BAKING AND MAKING DESSERTS
text:
1. Tightens the gluten structure

Salt has a binding or strengthening effect on gluten — this allows the dough to rise and expand during baking. It’s indispensable, for example, when baking bread, pastries, croissants or sponges.

- It’s impossible to get a tall sponge without adding salt to the batter. Salted batter will turn out more voluminous and stronger than unsalted.

2. Enhances the taste

Salt brings out the characteristic taste of pastry it is used in. When used in moderate amounts, it does not make the product taste salty, but simply enhances its best qualities. It turns insipid two-dimensional tastes into rich, three-dimensional ones.

Such an effect is achieved thanks to the right combination of different tastes. For example, when salt is added, sweet flavors become less sweet and more complex, while sour flavors become less prominent.

3. Neutralize bitterness

Salt neutralizes bitterness, so any bitter foods (e.g. coffee, dark chocolate, grapefruit) become more appetizing and tasty if you add a little salt.

- Grapefruit remains slightly bitter both fresh and baked even after removing the albedo (the whitish, spongy inner part of the rind of a citrus fruit). But salting the pulp helps to get rid of this specific aftertaste.

4. Stabilizes the egg white foam

It’s thanks to the addition of that tiny pinch of salt that the egg whites, when whipped, start to increase in volume and become lush. Adding salt to your meringue will ensure that all of the protein chains have safely bonded together.

A similar effect can be obtained by adding acid (e.g. lemon juice).
part 2

Judging by your comments, this topic turned out to be interesting for many of you. Today we’ll continue to talk about the functions of salt. We have already analyzed the first four functions (check out the beginning by following the hashtag #marusya_about_salt), but that's not all

So let's continue.

part 3

Continuing to delve into the topic of infusion, today we take into account the hot method, that I use quite often when developing recipes.

title: HOT METHOD
text:
Many of you, probably, have guessed that the hot method involves heat treatment. You’re on the right track. Hot infusion consists in bringing the liquid together with spices, herbs or other flavorings to a boil, followed by infusion for 30-60 minutes.

The infused liquid can be cream, milk or berry puree. For example, you can infuse the cream with dry lavender, as I did in Blueberry-Lavender Cheesecake (photo 3-6), or you can give a mouthwatering coffee aroma by hot infusion the cream with ground cofee (Coffee-Baileys Cheesecake, photo 7-8).

Everything is very simple, but there are secrets that I will gladly share with you.

title: HOT METHOD SECRETS
text:
- The infused liquid must be heated over medium or low heat so that the heating occurs gradually.
- In the infusion process, I advise you to use as few dishes as possible to prepare ingredients. For example, it is better to remove the zest immediately into cream. Don’t remove the zest on the board, and then transfer it to cream from the board, as all spices, herbs and citrus fruits contain a large amount of essential oils which evaporate easily.
- After boiling, you must immediately remove the saucepan from the heat - at too high temperatures, flavors can release substances that will negatively affect the flavor and aroma.
- After heating, it is better to cover the liquid with a cling film in contact. If you cover it with a lid, excess moisture from evaporation will form on it, which will get into the liquid. Furthermore, skin which you will need to remove will be formed.
- After infusion, don’t forget to strain it through a sieve or cheesecloth.
- The infused liquid can be stored in the refrigerator after complete cooling during the shelf life of the main product. Keep in mind that the resulting flavor will evaporate with each day of storage!

Did you learn something new for yourself today? If yes, let me know in the comments
5. Balances sweetness

Salt helps to balance the taste of products with a pronounced sweetness, such as caramel, chocolate or meringue. Such products are usually treacly, and it’s almost impossible to add other flavor accents to them, even if you think they will work well in your pastry. Salt added in low concentrations balances the sweetness and adds depth to other flavors, so that our taste buds perceive them as moderately sweet, although the amount of sugar remains unchanged.

6. Helps to release juices

Salt changes the balance of liquid in foods. It makes juicy berries and fruits release juices, leaving the fibrous material behind. If you are making a fruit dessert and you need to get the maximum juice, just add a pinch of salt to your fruits.

7. Increases the shelf life

Salt is a natural preservative. It dehydrates harmful microorganisms. Due to dehydration, bacteria become inactive, their growth stops, the metabolism of their cells becomes impossible, which is why they die. Different types of microorganisms become harmless at different salt concentrations. But even in a small amount, salt increases the shelf life of pastry.

8. Helps to maintain the recommended daily sodium intake

Our body needs a certain amount of salt (NaCl) to function properly, so it's natural that we tend to like the taste of salt. This does not mean that we should eat tons of salt a day, but using it in reasonable amounts in cooking and making desserts will help us stay healthy and enjoy food.

title: INFUSION: WHAT, BY WHAT AND HOW
text:
#marusya_infusion

part 4 (the last one)

We have already talked with you about the cold and hot method of infusion. Today I will tell you about decoction and vacuuming.

title: DECOCTION
text:
This method, of course, is very similar to hot method — the liquid is also subjected to heat treatment. However, there is one significant difference — with hot method, we only heat the liquid or bring it to a boil, but as for decoction, we boil for several minutes or even cook for up to 60 minutes to get dense aromatic decoctions.
Infusions are steeped and decoctions are simmered.

If we talk about confectionery, this method is often used in the preparation of flavored sugar syrups for coating muffins or, for example, soaking sponge cake.

For the preparation of fillings for honey cakes "Fig-Parmesan-Gorgonzola-Red Wine" and "Quince-Goat Cheese-Medium Sweet White Wine" we also use this method — juicy fleshy figs and fragrant quince are stewed in wine from 25 to 60 minutes until the liquid has almost completely evaporated. Due to the prolonged exposure to high temperature, we get incredibly tasty, rich and fragrant fillings!

title: VACUUMING
text:
This is a method for infusion of solid ingredients (bananas, mangoes, coconut, pineapple, apples, etc.), which are subsequently used as whole or cut.

Thanks to vacuuming, we can give the main product a lot of flavors!

There are several ways:

1. Take a dense main ingredient and pour it with juice of the infusing one, then leave to infuse in the refrigerator.
2. Mix the main and infusing ingredients — you can even wrap apple pieces with lemon slices or thin mango strips, sprinkled with cinnamon or other spices. After that, it is necessary to place them in a bag for vacuuming and pump out the air with a vacuum cleaner.

As a result, you can get an orange-flavored apple, for example, or a lemon-flavored banana.

title: EVERYTHING YOU NEED TO KNOW ABOUT AGAR
text:
part 1

In previous posts, we have already talked with you about gelatin - #marusya_about_gelatin and pectin - #marusya_about_pectin. Today I suggest analyzing the next, no less interesting thickener - agar, aka agar-agar, aka seaweed food thickener.

Agar means "seaweed" in Malaysian. Its gelling properties are said to be accidentally discovered in Japan in the 17th century by Mino Tarōzaemon. He found out that the chilled seaweed soup had a jelly-like consistency the next day.

Agar is extracted from red and brown algae, which undergo several stages of rinsing, drying and grinding.

Nowadays, this natural thickener is widely used in confectionery art. It’s used to make zephyr, marmalade, fruit pastes (pastila), sweets, jelly and mousse desserts.

Agar can be classified by its quality and gel strength.

title: Quality
text:
- High grade agar - has a white or light yellow color, although it can have a slightly grayish tint
- First grade agar - varies from yellow to dark yellow color

title: Gel strength
text:
- 600-1200 g/cm2

The higher the number it has, the thicker gel can be obtained. The greater the strength of agar is, the less amount of it is needed to gel the mixture.

- You can check out the table that shows how to convert between different amounts of agar-agar depending on the gel strength in the carousel.

Agar is often referred to as a natural substitute for gelatin. However, these two thickeners have a number of differences.

title: AGAR VS GELATIN
text:
1. Unlike gelatin, agar does not impart any taste, smell, or color to desserts.
2. In terms of gelling properties, agar is 10 times superior to gelatin
3. Unlike gelatin, agar activates in an acidic environment. Gelatin is not a good choice when it comes to preparing, for example, desserts with pineapple or kiwi - they contain enzymes that destroy proteins (87-92% of the composition of gelatin). But agar-agar perfectly gels such mixtures.
4. Unlike gelatin, agar is thermoreversible - it can be heated and frozen as many times as you like.
part 2

Please support this useful post with your like ー this is extremely important for us now!

For those interested in the answer to the question from the previous post about using agar to make the orange confit for the “Orange-Dark Chocolate" honey cake: I chose it because the filling made with gelatin began to leak out after defrosting.

This is due to the fact that ice crystals formed in the orange confit during freezing, which broke the texture of the jelly. As a result, the filling lost its original properties and began to leak out after defrosting.

Will gelatin-based filling always leak out after defrosting? No, it won’t. Moreover, sometimes after defrosting, a filling made with agar or pectin may also leak out. What does it depend on? First of all, it depends on the amount of unbound water in the composition, but this should be discussed in another post.

Today we’ll continue examining the agar. So, here are the RULES OF WORKING WITH AGAR:

1. Agar does not dissolve in cold water ー it should be brought to 95-100 °C to completely dissolve, at this temperature it forms a viscous and transparent solution, which when cooled to 35-40 °C, turns into a thick and pure gel.

2. Agar does not require pre-soaking in water or mixing with sugar. In order to introduce agar into the mixture, it is enough just to add it in there! The mixture can be hot, warm or cold ー it does not matter.

3. Agar is a thermoreversible thickener. You can heat and freeze fillings made with it as many times as you like ー it won't lose its gelling properties.

4. One of the main advantages of agar over gelatin is the ability to activate in an acidic environment. The advantage over pectin is that agar gels well even in the absence of sugar in the mixture.

5. The thicker the desired consistency of the gel you want to obtain is, the stronger agar should be used and / or the more agar you need.
part 3

Today we’ll talk about how to correctly calculate the required amount of agar and what it depends on.

If you are making a dessert with agar using a recipe from an eminent chef, in order to get a stable result, be sure to pay attention to:

- amount of agar — agar is a very strong thickener (10 times stronger than gelatin), so even a slight deviation of 0.1-0.2 g can change the texture of the gel
- strength of agar — if the recipe says "5 g of agar 1200", to get a dessert "like from a chef" you need to either use agar of the same strength or use the one that is available and convert between its strength.

- you can find the table that shows how to convert between different amounts of agar-agar depending on the gel strength in the 1st post from the series #marusya_about_agar.

- agar brand (if specified) — as a rule, despite the same strength, agar of different brands can slightly differ in the opacity / transparency of the gel obtained and gelling properties, so it is best to stick to a brand recommended by chef.

If you use a recipe from the Internet, where there’s no information about the strength of the agar used, or you want to create a dessert yourself, take into account the following tips:

title: Recommended dosage
text:
2-4 g of agar per 150-180 ml of liquid

The exact amount depends on:

- liquid being gelled and its acidity

The higher the acidity of the liquid is, the more agar must be added. This is due to the fact that acid lowers the gelling properties of thickeners, including agar. For example, to gel 100 ml of a neutral liquid (e.g. water, milk) you’ll need 0.9-1 g of agar, while for 100 ml of an acidic liquid (e.g. juice) — 1.3-1.5 g of agar.

- desired texture

runny texture — 0.8 g / 500 ml
soft texture — 1.5 g / 500 ml
thick texture — 5 g / 500 ml
very thick texture — 7 g / 500 ml

If this post was useful for you, leave any comment or emoticon under it — I’ll be very pleased
#marusya_about_agar

part 4

Today will be the final part of a series of articles about agar. I’ll tell you about the terms and conditions of storage, as well as possible agar substitutes.

title: Agar
text:
The shelf life of agar varies from 2 to 3 years since the date of packaging. It is indicated on the packaging and may change depending on the formula and production technology of agar by a specific manufacturer.

Agar should be stored in a cool, dry place, protected from sunlight, in airtight packaging.

- Products with agar

1. Agar-based confectionery products are stored about 24 to 36 hours at a temperature between +4 to -8°C
2. Fruit mixtures — up to 7 days in the refrigerator
3. Jam and other preservation — up to 1 month in a cool, dry place, protected from sunlight

title: Gelatin
text:
Gelatin has a lower density after cooling than agar, so it is suitable for making more delicate desserts. If you want to get a dense and smooth texture, it is better to use agar.

In general, these thickeners can be considered interchangeable, but it should be kept in mind that the gelling ability of agar is much higher than that of gelatin.

- Substitute: 1 tsp. agar = 2-3 tsp. gelatin

ℹ It’s not suitable for vegetarians, as gelatin is made from the bones and tendons of animals

title: Pectin
text:
Pectin is the most beneficial and equivalent substitute for agar, but there are exceptions. Both products have the vegetal nature and the only difference is that pectin contains carbohydrates, and its calorie content is higher than that of agar.

A prerequisite for the "activation" of pectin is the presence of sugar. Accordingly, substitute agar for pectin in the making of sugar-free desserts is impossible.

- Substitute: 1 tsp. agar = 2-3 tsp. pectin

title: Corn Starch
text:
Agar-agar can be substituted for starch. However, starch makes the filling opaque, when dissolved, that significantly narrows the range of its possibilities.

- Substitute: 1 tsp. agar = 2 tsp. starch

title: BROWN BUTTER OR BEURRE NOISETTE
text:
#marusya_theory_tips

In the comments under yesterday's post, I noticed that for some people the technique of making brown butter was new and it raised questions and doubts.

Therefore, today I decided to share with you my tips and tricks in order to dispel your doubts and inspire you to make incredibly delicious blackberry, bilberry and star anise cupcakes while the berry season is in full swing.

Brown or browned butter (fr. beurre noisette) are all different names for the same product obtained by heating regular butter - it melts, separates into butterfat and milk solids, the latter sink to the bottom of the pan and turn a deep brown color.

The browning (caramelization) of butter is the result of the milk proteins and sugars going through the Maillard reaction upon heating to 130 °C.

The recipe for brown butter can be found in the previous post. But I’d like to give you some tips so that everything goes perfectly, and you don’t get nervous.

title: 6 TIPS FOR GETTING THE PERFECT BEURRE NOISETTE
text:
1. Use a thick-bottomed saucepan to ensure even heating of the butter.

2. The saucepan should be of a light color - it’s more difficult to notice the change in the color of the butter against a dark background, and it can easily burn.

3. To get the perfect brown butter, I advise you to heat no more than 200 g of butter at a time in a small saucepan (d = 14-16 cm). If you need a larger amount, use a saucepan d = 22-26 cm.

4. When the butter gets frothy, start to constantly stir it with a whisk so that the milk solids do not burn.

5. After bringing the butter to 128 °C, remove the saucepan from the heat, while continuing to stir - within 30-40 seconds the residual heat of the saucepan will bring the butter to the desired slightly brownish color (it will heat up to 130-138 °C).

6. Immediately after this, pour the butter into a separate container to stop the cooking process. Otherwise, the temperature will continue to rise, and as soon as it exceeds 140 °C, the butter will burn.

title: NFUSION. THE INS AND OUTS
text:
#marusya_infusion
part 1

At first glance, the topic is very simple and there is nothing to talk about. But! You will be surprised when you find out that even when I was giving a master class at a large-scale production, the guys were perplexed by my advice to change the method of infusion to cold.

In fact, aroma and taste are inextricably linked, and they should be considered as a whole.
